title: Taller caps
translation: Someone once told me: "Court caps these days are far taller than they used to be." If you have an old cap box, you have to add a strip to the rim before you can use it now.
original: 「このごろの{冠|かぶり}は、{昔|むかし}よりは{遥|はる}かに{高|たか}くなりたるなり。」とぞ、ある{人|ひと}おほせられし。
{古代|こたい}の{冠桶|かぶりをけ}を{持|も}ちたる{人|ひと}は、{端|はた}をつぎて{今|いま}は{用|もち}ふるなり。
literal: 'The caps of recent times have become far taller than in the old days', someone said.
People who own an old-style cap box add on to the edge and use it now.

notes.text: {冠|かぶり}: the stiff black lacquered cap that men wore at court with formal dress. The 1925 edition reads it かぶり; かうぶり and かんむり are other readings of the same word.
The same frame as section 64: someone of high rank told Kenkō in person (おほす respectful, き past experienced).
A lacquered box for keeping the cap. The old boxes were made for lower caps, so the new caps did not fit.
{端|はた}: the edge, the rim. つぐ: 'to join on, to extend'. The fashion is visible in the furniture: the boxes had to grow with the caps.
{用|もち}ふ is a later form of {用|もち}ゐる 'to use', common in Kenkō's time. Section 63 has it too: {用|もち}ひむ.
